title: Troubleshoot Motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and Power

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Motherboard, RAM, CPU, cooling, and power problems can produce similar symptoms. CompTIA expects you to recognize the symptom first and connect it to the most likely hardware area.
bullets: POST beeps and proprietary crash screens
Blank screen and no power
Sluggish performance and overheating
Burning smell and random shutdown
Application crashes and unusual noise
Capacitor swelling
Inaccurate system date/time
sections.callout: OBSERVE → ISOLATE → CONNECT THE SYMPTOM TO POWER, RAM, CPU, COOLING, OR MOTHERBOARD

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a computer fails, use the symptom to determine which motherboard, RAM, CPU, cooling, or power component should be investigated first.
bullets: POST beep pattern → startup hardware problem
No power → start with the power path
Power but no image → blank-screen path
Slow and hot → thermal issue
Shutdown under load → power or overheating
Burning smell → electrical overheating or failure
Bulging capacitor → motherboard damage
Date/time resets → CMOS/RTC battery

sections.title: Common Motherboard, RAM, CPU, and Power Symptoms
paragraphs: Troubleshooting questions usually describe an effect instead of naming the failed component. Do not immediately replace hardware; identify when the symptom appears and which subsystem could produce it.
sections.callout: SYMPTOM → LIKELY AREA → VERIFY

sections.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
bullets: What exactly is the symptom?
When does it occur?
Does the computer receive power?
Does POST complete?
Is the problem constant or intermittent?
Is heat involved?
Did hardware recently change?
sections.callout: Gather evidence before replacing components.

sections.title: Power-On Self-Test (POST)
paragraphs: During startup, firmware performs a Power-On Self-Test to confirm essential hardware is available and functioning well enough to continue. RAM, CPU, motherboard, and video problems can be detected during POST.
sections.callout: POST = hardware check before normal boot.

sections.title: POST Beeps
paragraphs: When a system cannot display an error, firmware may report hardware problems through beep patterns. Codes vary by motherboard and firmware manufacturer, so use the manufacturer's documentation rather than assuming a universal chart.
sections.callout: Repeating beeps after a RAM installation → verify RAM seating and compatibility, then consult the system's beep-code documentation.

sections.title: POST Beeps vs. Operating-System Errors
sections.callout: BEFORE OS → POST.

sections.title: Proprietary Crash Screens
paragraphs: Platforms may display proprietary crash screens after severe system errors. The screen signals instability but does not by itself identify one failed component. Record error information, recent changes, repeated patterns, and whether crashes occur under load.
sections.callout: Crash screen = symptom requiring investigation.

sections.title: Blank Screen
paragraphs: A blank screen can occur even though the computer appears to start. Investigate system power, monitor and video connections, RAM, GPU, motherboard, CPU, and POST failure. First determine whether the computer is actually powering on.
sections.callout: LIGHTS/FANS BUT NO IMAGE → BLANK-SCREEN PATH.

sections.title: RAM and a Blank Screen
paragraphs: Improperly seated or incompatible RAM can prevent POST. If a blank screen begins after a RAM upgrade, power down, verify compatibility and correct slots, reseat the modules, and test known-good memory when appropriate.
sections.callout: Hardware changed → inspect the changed hardware first.

sections.title: No Power
paragraphs: No power means the system shows no normal signs of starting: no LEDs, fans, POST, display, or startup sounds. Follow the path from the wall outlet through any power strip or UPS, power cord, PSU switch, PSU connections, motherboard connectors, and front-panel power connection.
sections.callout: No power → follow electricity from the wall to the motherboard.

sections.callout: DEAD MACHINE → POWER. RUNNING MACHINE, NO PICTURE → DISPLAY/POST/HARDWARE.

sections.title: Sluggish Performance
paragraphs: Within this objective, sluggish performance can involve insufficient RAM, CPU performance, overheating, thermal throttling, or hardware instability. A system that slows as temperatures rise may be reducing CPU performance for protection.
sections.callout: Fast when cold but slow after heavy use → investigate overheating.

sections.title: Insufficient RAM and Performance
paragraphs: When RAM is insufficient, the operating system may depend more heavily on storage-based virtual memory, making the system feel sluggish. Use the complete scenario rather than blaming RAM for every slow system.
sections.callout: Not enough working memory → performance can suffer.

sections.title: Overheating
paragraphs: Cooling failures can cause sluggish performance, instability, application crashes, and random shutdowns. Inspect fans, heat sinks, dust, thermal paste or pads, airflow, pumps, and CPU temperature.
sections.callout: HEAT → THROTTLE → CRASH → SHUT DOWN, depending on severity.

sections.title: Common Causes of Overheating
bullets: Failed fan
Blocked airflow
Dust buildup
Loose heat sink
Improperly installed cooler
Dried or improperly applied thermal material
Failed liquid-cooling pump
sections.callout: Temperature rises rapidly after cooler replacement → verify cooler seating and the thermal interface.

sections.title: Burning Smell
paragraphs: A burning smell is a serious warning that can indicate PSU failure, a short circuit, overheated wiring, motherboard component failure, or a damaged connector. If safe, remove power before inspection and do not keep operating the computer to see whether the smell disappears.
sections.callout: Burning electrical odor → power down and investigate hardware and power.

sections.title: Random Shutdown
paragraphs: A sudden power-off can result from overheating, PSU failure, insufficient power, motherboard faults, or other serious instability. If it happens during heavy CPU or GPU load, check temperatures and PSU capability.
sections.callout: Shutdown under load → heat or power become strong suspects.

sections.title: Application Crashes
paragraphs: One application may have a software problem, but repeated unpredictable crashes across unrelated applications can suggest faulty RAM, CPU instability, overheating, or wider system instability.
sections.callout: One app → perhaps the app. Many unrelated apps → consider system instability.

sections.title: RAM and Application Crashes
paragraphs: Faulty RAM can corrupt data while programs run, causing application crashes, system crashes, random errors, and instability.
sections.callout: Multiple applications crash randomly with no clear software pattern → test RAM.

sections.title: Unusual Noise
paragraphs: Locate unusual noises before deciding what failed. In this objective, sources include cooling fans, the PSU fan, liquid-cooling pumps, and obstructed fan blades. Drive clicking or grinding belongs to storage troubleshooting under Objective 5.2.
sections.callout: Find where the sound originates.

sections.title: Fan Noise
paragraphs: A fan may become loud because its bearings are failing, dust or a cable is touching the blades, or it is running at maximum speed because temperatures are high.
sections.callout: A loud fan may be the problem or a clue to another heat problem.

sections.title: Capacitor Swelling
paragraphs: Failed capacitors on motherboards or other hardware may bulge, swell, or leak. An obviously swollen top is a physical hardware-failure clue, not a software problem.
sections.callout: BULGING CAPACITOR → MOTHERBOARD FAILURE.

sections.title: Inaccurate System Date/Time
paragraphs: A small motherboard battery supports the real-time clock and certain firmware settings when normal power is unavailable. A weak CMOS/RTC battery can cause the date, time, or BIOS/UEFI settings to reset.
sections.callout: Clock forgets after power removal → CMOS/RTC battery.

sections.title: Date/Time vs. Network Time Issue
paragraphs: A clock that becomes wrong only while the OS is running may involve synchronization or software. If stored time repeatedly disappears after the system is unplugged, the motherboard battery is a strong suspect.
sections.callout: FORGETS WHEN UNPLUGGED → BATTERY.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Beeps before the OS loads → POST hardware error
Exact beep meaning → manufacturer documentation
System powers up but shows no picture → blank screen
No LEDs or fans → no power
System slows as temperature rises → overheating or thermal throttling
Electrical burning odor → remove power and investigate
Shutdown during heavy load → power or overheating
Unrelated programs crash → possible RAM or system instability
Grinding or rattling from cooling area → fan or cooling problem
Bulging motherboard component → capacitor swelling
Time lost after unplugging → CMOS/RTC battery

sections.title: Objective 5.1 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Distinguish failure to receive power, failure to POST, thermal instability, and component failure before choosing an action.

entries.title: No Power vs. Blank Screen
paragraphs: No lights and no fans follow the power path. Lights or fans with no image follow the blank-screen and POST path.
entries.memoryHook: NO LIFE → POWER | LIFE, NO IMAGE → POST/DISPLAY

entries.title: POST Beep vs. OS Crash
paragraphs: A beep during initial startup belongs to POST. A crash after the OS loads is a runtime problem.

entries.title: RAM vs. CPU Heat
paragraphs: Random application crashes make RAM a strong possibility; performance that falls as temperature rises points toward CPU overheating or thermal throttling.

entries.title: Overheating vs. Insufficient PSU
paragraphs: High temperature points toward cooling. Shutdown after adding high-power hardware can point toward an inadequate PSU.

entries.title: Burning Smell vs. Overheating
paragraphs: High temperature calls for cooling checks. A burning electrical odor requires power-down and hardware inspection.

entries.title: Unusual Noise
paragraphs: Fan or pump noise belongs to cooling and power troubleshooting. Drive clicking or grinding belongs to Objective 5.2.

entries.title: Capacitor Swelling
paragraphs: Swollen or leaking capacitors are a physical motherboard-failure symptom.

entries.title: Inaccurate Date/Time
paragraphs: Firmware time that resets after loss of power points toward the CMOS/RTC battery.

sections.title: Hardware Symptom Workflow
bullets: Observe the exact symptom and when it occurs.
Separate no-power, POST, runtime, thermal, and physical-warning paths.
Check recent hardware changes first.
Use manufacturer documentation for proprietary indicators such as beep codes.
Verify the likely component or subsystem before replacement.
Protect the system and remove power when electrical damage is suspected.
sections.callout: OBSERVE → ISOLATE → VERIFY

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Startup beep pattern → POST error
Powered system with no image → blank screen
No lights or fans → no power
Performance slows as heat rises → thermal throttling
Very high temperatures → cooling problem
Burning electrical odor → power down and investigate
Sudden shutdown under load → power or overheating
Random application crashes → possible faulty RAM
Rattling cooling fan → fan problem
Bulging capacitor → motherboard failure
Date/time resets after power removal → CMOS/RTC battery
sections.callout: NO POWER → FOLLOW POWER | NO DISPLAY → CHECK POST | RANDOM ERRORS → CONSIDER RAM | HOT + SLOW → THERMAL | BURNING → STOP POWER | FORGOTTEN TIME → BATTERY
